newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Tension hangs over final NATO forum before Madrid.
newsitem.headline: Tension hangs over final NATO forum before Madrid.

text.p: A NATO security meeting starting in Prague this weekend has become a last chance forum for would-be members whose hopes have been dashed by the United States.
Officially the new membership decisions lie with leaders of the Western military alliance at their July 8-9 summit in Madrid.

But President Bill Clinton stole the summit's thunder last week by announcing Washington's "firm" position that only Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic should be invited into NATO's first round of expansion into former communist Eastern Europe.

Disappointed aspirants Romania and Slovenia are hoping their backers can turn up the diplomatic heat on their behalf at the 14th NATO Workshop, an informal East-West discussion of security and political issues among ministers, military experts and diplomats.
France and Italy are the leading challengers to the U.S. diktat.
But the alliance operates by consensus and the three U.S. choices appear to be the only ones which all 16 members would support. So a larger expansion appears unlikely this time.
"Getting a consensus among 16 countries is very difficult and ot have expected that this time it would have been smooth sailing," Czech deputy foreign minister Karel Kovanda told Reuters.
"The (U.S. position) is the largest common denominator, isn't it?" he added.
Washington says that NATO membership should remain indefinitely open to any European country not selected in Madrid, and much of the talk in Prague will be about what happens after the first round.
The workshop will also give top Czech officials like President Vaclav Havel a chance to showcase the benefits of NATO membership for their reluctant citizens.

Opinion polls show that still fewer than half of Czechs want to join the alliance, the lowest support among the three top aspirants, even though NATO membership has been a top post-Communist priority of the Prague government.
A key focus of the Prague workshop will be Romanian President Emil Constantinescu's appearance on Monday, where he is expected to make a final appeal for membership.

Michael Shafir, a Romania political analyst based in Prague, said that Constantinescu's real aim would probably be to lay the groundwork for later inclusion by showing that the three U.S.-backed new members want the Romanians in.
"They get along very well with the Hungarians, well with the Poles, and probably less so with the Czechs," Shafir said.
A delegation from the small former Yugoslav republic Slovenia, one of the most rapidly reforming ex-Communist countries, will be headed by Foreign Minister Zoran Thaler.

"I'm sure the minister will use the opportunity to talk to influential NATO representatives in line with his claim that Slovenia will pursue a diplomatic offensive for NATO until the Madrid conference," a diplomat said in Ljubljana.
"The success of his mission will however depend upon the influence of people that will participate at the Prague workshop," he added.
The highest U.S. official attending the Prague conference will be Deputy Secretary of Defence John White.
